title: Delhi High Court Rules OpenAI's AI Training on ANI News Is Fair Dealing
excerpt: In a landmark order, the Delhi High Court declined to grant ANI interim relief in its copyright suit against OpenAI, holding that using news content to train ChatGPT falls under India's fair-dealing exemption.
body:
The Delhi High Court on Friday ruled that OpenAI's use of news agency ANI's copyrighted content to train its ChatGPT models does not amount to copyright infringement, in what is the first substantive judicial finding in India on the intersection of AI training and copyright law.

https://x.com/IndianExpress/status/2080582317018652872

Justice Amit Bansal declined to grant ANI Media Pvt Ltd an interim injunction against OpenAI, holding that the storage of copyrighted news articles for training large language models falls under Section 52(1)(a) of India's Copyright Act — the fair-dealing exemption for research.

  • Delhi High Court held that OpenAI's use of ANI's news content for AI training constitutes fair dealing under Section 52(1)(a) of India's Copyright Act
  • Justice Amit Bansal found ANI failed to show ChatGPT memorised or reproduced its news reports, declining to grant an interim injunction
  • The order is the first substantive finding by an Indian constitutional court on AI training and copyright
  • The copyright suit remains pending; this ruling addresses only interim relief, not the final merits of the case

What the Court Said

The court found that ANI failed to establish a prima facie case that ChatGPT had memorised or reproduced its news reports. Justice Bansal observed that responses generated by ChatGPT — including those using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — were not substantially similar to ANI's original content.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=7CkYc0VhJzE

"ANI has failed to make a prima facie case for interim injunction."

— Justice Amit Bansal, Delhi High Court

The court also ruled that the balance of convenience favoured OpenAI, noting that an interim injunction would cause "irreparable injury" not only to the company but also to the public at large.

Background of the Case

ANI sued OpenAI in the Delhi High Court in November 2024, accusing the US company of using its published content without permission to train its AI models. The news agency also alleged that ChatGPT attributed fabricated stories to ANI — so-called AI "hallucinations" — which it argued damaged its reputation.

OpenAI denied the allegations and challenged the maintainability of the suit in India, arguing that its models are not trained in the country and its servers are located outside India. The company also said it had blocklisted ANI's domain from future training since November 2024 and had refined its models to prevent regurgitation of training data.

During earlier hearings, OpenAI told the court that any order to remove training data would conflict with its legal obligations in the United States, where it faces similar litigation, according to Reuters.

A Precedent-Setting Order

The observation on fair dealing is the first of its kind by an Indian constitutional court, according to Madhyamam. While the order does not decide the merits of the case — the copyright suit remains pending — it gives OpenAI an important procedural win by allowing it to continue operating without restrictions during the trial.

The ruling comes as courts worldwide grapple with the same question: whether AI companies can train their models on copyrighted content without a licence. OpenAI faces similar lawsuits in the United States, including a high-profile case brought by The New York Times, and in Canada. Friday's order in Delhi marks one of the first times a court outside the US has weighed in substantively on the issue.

Wider Industry Impact

The case has drawn attention far beyond ANI and OpenAI. Several Indian publishers, including NDTV, Network18, The Indian Express, and Hindustan Times, sought to join ANI's legal battle. Music labels such as T-Series, Saregama, and Sony Music also sought to intervene, arguing that AI companies should not be allowed to use copyrighted works without permission or licensing.

For India's media industry — and the global Indian-language content ecosystem — the ruling raises difficult questions. If AI training on published content is protected as fair dealing, news organisations and content creators may have limited legal recourse to control how their work is used by AI systems.

OpenAI had argued that publishers who do not want their content used for training can prevent web crawlers from accessing their websites, effectively placing the burden on rights holders rather than AI companies.

What Comes Next

The copyright suit remains pending before the Delhi High Court. Friday's order addressed only ANI's request for interim relief, not the underlying question of whether OpenAI's use of ANI's content constitutes copyright infringement on the merits.

As the case proceeds to trial, it will likely set the framework for how Indian courts handle the growing tension between AI development and intellectual property rights — a question with significant implications for India's technology sector, its media industry, and the millions of Indian users who rely on AI tools daily.
nri_angle: The ruling sets a precedent for how Indian copyright law applies to AI training, with implications for Indian media companies and the broader tech ecosystem that serves Indian users globally.
